description:
What changes when the curse is finally removed from the earth? Wesam Saad follows the previous study of creation’s redemption by examining the connection between Adam’s sin, painful toil and Christ’s redeeming work. Genesis 3 supplies the starting point: the ground is cursed, work brings frustration, and human life ends in death. The crown of thorns is then considered alongside the teaching that Christ became a curse for his people.

The distinction between present and future salvation is central. Believers can know forgiveness now while still living amid the effects of the curse. Revelation 22 points beyond that present experience to a world where the curse is absent and God’s people serve him. Wesam argues that removing the curse restores creation and its intended activity rather than making physical existence unnecessary.

Much of the discussion explores work and relationships in that future life. The teacher distinguishes useful effort from miserable toil and moral perfection from possessing unlimited knowledge. He presents cooperation, learning and patient dealings with others as implications of that distinction, while acknowledging unanswered questions about bodily details. The prospect is intended to deepen longing for life with Christ: purposeful service, shared joy and fellowship freed from sin, rather than an eternity imagined as empty inactivity.

questions.question: What does Genesis 3 show about the curse on the ground?
questions.answer: Wesam highlights the connection between Adam’s sin and the difficult conditions of life and work. Thorns, thistles, painful labour and eventual death describe a creation no longer functioning as it originally did. He distinguishes this misery from effort itself: useful work existed before the fall, so the curse should not be identified with every form of demanding activity.

questions.question: How does the crown of thorns contribute to the study’s account of redemption?
questions.answer: The thorns associated with the cursed ground reappear in the crown placed on Jesus. Wesam connects that image with the teaching that Christ became a curse for his people. He uses the connection to explain Christ bearing the consequences brought through Adam, and to focus attention on the cost of redemption rather than treating the lifting of the curse as a detached improvement to the world.

questions.question: Why distinguish forgiveness now from the removal of the curse in the future?
questions.answer: Believers are forgiven through Christ now, but their gardens still grow weeds and their lives still contain pain and frustration. Wesam warns against collapsing present and future benefits into a single experience. Christ’s work grounds present reconciliation and the future removal of the curse, when the misery described in Genesis will no longer dominate the renewed creation.

questions.question: Does removal of the curse mean the end of work?
questions.answer: Work does not cease when the curse is removed. Wesam expects service and purposeful activity to continue. The change is the removal of miserable toil, sin and frustration, rather than the elimination of every demanding task. He uses cultivation and enjoyable physical effort to distinguish hard work from painful futility, and argues that future work will be disciplined and fruitful instead of reluctant or half-hearted.

questions.question: Does sinlessness mean that people possess God’s unlimited knowledge?
questions.answer: Wesam distinguishes moral perfection from knowing everything. He reasons that people who remain finite can continue to learn and may misunderstand information without intending evil. His examples of practical mistakes are proposed implications of that distinction, rather than direct descriptions of a particular event in the new earth. They must not be confused with a claim that sin continues there.

questions.question: Why does the discussion emphasise cooperation and patience?
questions.answer: If people learn and work together, they will benefit from one another’s knowledge. Wesam pictures that cooperation freed from pride, bitterness and sinful reactions, so that correction can be offered and received with love. He connects this expectation with the commands to bear with and build up one another. The illustrations express his reasoning about fellowship, not a detailed blueprint of future jobs.

questions.question: What limits does Wesam acknowledge when questions turn to bodily details?
questions.answer: He does not claim definite knowledge about every physical condition, such as whether glorified people could receive a cut or how bodily replenishment will work. Some possibilities are discussed, but he distinguishes traceable implications from matters he cannot establish. Those unanswered details remain uncertain, so conversational suggestions should not be treated as promises about the future body.

questions.question: How is future fellowship presented as an enlargement of joy?
questions.answer: The discussion does not portray the end of marriage as the destruction of every good friendship. Wesam argues that fellowship in Christ will be deepened and widened beyond the present family unit, without the sinful dependence that can distort relationships now. His closing emphasis is on more shared joy, not less, encouraging listeners to long for life together in Christ’s presence.
